author: original (NevaIB)
title: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
themeLabel: Models of the particulate nature of matter
islUnits: 1. Atomic theory and kinetic theory (Y12 Sep)
bigPicture: Everything is made of particles. Whether those particles are single elements, fixed-ratio compounds or loose mixtures decides how we can separate them, and how fast the particles move (their kinetic energy) decides the state. Temperature in kelvin is a direct measure of that average kinetic energy.

keyIdeas.cue: Element vs compound vs mixture, and how do you separate mixtures?
keyIdeas.answer: Element: one type of atom, cannot be broken down chemically. Compound: two or more elements bonded in a fixed ratio; properties differ from the elements. Mixture: substances not bonded, any ratio, separable by physical methods. Homogeneous mixtures have one uniform phase (salt water); heterogeneous ones have visibly separate phases (sand in water). Methods: dissolve (solvation) then filter an insoluble solid; evaporate or recrystallise to recover a dissolved solid; distil to separate liquids by boiling point; paper chromatography for coloured mixtures.

keyIdeas.cue: How does the kinetic molecular model explain states and changes of state?
keyIdeas.answer: Solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions, strong attractions. Liquid: particles close together but able to move past each other. Gas: particles far apart, moving fast and randomly. Changes: melting/freezing (s↔l), vaporisation (evaporation at the surface or boiling throughout) and condensation (l↔g), sublimation and deposition (s↔g). Write state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) in equations.

keyIdeas.cue: What does temperature measure, and what happens on a heating curve?
keyIdeas.answer: Absolute temperature (K) is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles. T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C. On a heating curve the flat sections are changes of state: energy goes into overcoming attractions (potential energy), not into raising kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.

keyIdeas.cue: Which property does each separation technique rely on?
keyIdeas.answer: Filtration: particle size (insoluble solid vs liquid). Solvation/dissolving: solubility. Evaporation and crystallisation: the solvent is volatile, the solute is not. Distillation: different boiling points. Paper chromatography: different attraction to the paper vs the solvent.

keyIdeas.cue: Do all particles in a sample have the same kinetic energy?
keyIdeas.answer: No. At any temperature there is a spread of speeds; temperature in kelvin is proportional to the average kinetic energy. At the same temperature, heavier particles move more slowly on average.

keyTerms.def: Substance made of one type of atom; cannot be split chemically.
Two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
Two or more substances not chemically bonded, in any ratio.
Uniform composition, single phase (e.g. air, brine).
Non-uniform; separate phases visible (e.g. oil and water).
Solid turning directly into gas (deposition is the reverse).
SI unit of temperature; 0 K is absolute zero, where particle kinetic energy is minimal.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a separation
workedExamples.prompt: How would you get pure, dry salt crystals from a mixture of sand and salt?
steps: Add water and stir: the salt dissolves, the sand does not.
Filter: sand stays on the filter paper, salt solution passes through as filtrate.
Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, then leave to cool so crystals form (recrystallisation).
Filter off the crystals and dry them.

misconceptions.wrong: A compound keeps the properties of its elements.
misconceptions.right: A compound has new properties: sodium (reactive metal) and chlorine (toxic gas) form harmless table salt.

misconceptions.wrong: Temperature rises steadily while ice melts.
misconceptions.right: Temperature stays constant during a change of state; the energy breaks attractions between particles.

misconceptions.wrong: Evaporation and boiling are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Both are vaporisation, but evaporation happens only at the surface and below the boiling point; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

misconceptions.wrong: (aq) is a fourth state of matter.
misconceptions.right: (aq) means dissolved in water; the states are solid, liquid and gas.

practice.prompt: Distinguish between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous mixture, with one example of each.
checkpoints: Homogeneous: uniform composition/one phase, e.g. salt solution
Heterogeneous: non-uniform, phases visible, e.g. sand and water

practice.prompt: Explain, using the kinetic molecular model, why the temperature of water stays at 100 °C while it boils.
checkpoints: Energy supplied is used to overcome intermolecular attractions
Average kinetic energy of molecules does not increase
So temperature (a measure of average Ek) stays constant until all liquid has vaporised

practice.prompt: Outline how paper chromatography could show whether a black ink is a single dye or a mixture.
checkpoints: Spot ink on a pencil baseline above solvent level, let solvent rise
More than one spot at different heights means a mixture

paper1A.why: Solid directly to gas. CO₂(g) → CO₂(s) is deposition.

paper1A.stem: A sample is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C. What is the change in temperature in kelvin?
paper1A.why: Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, so the change is the same number.
Fixed ratio of chemically bonded C and O; the others are mixtures.

paper1B.data: Heating curve data: a solid is heated at a constant rate. Temperature (°C) every minute: 20, 41, 62, 80, 80, 80, 80, 95, 110.
paper1B.prompt: State the melting point and explain the shape between minutes 3 and 6.
paper1B.answer: 80 °C. The flat section is melting: energy supplied overcomes attractions between particles, so average kinetic energy (temperature) does not rise.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Learn the six change-of-state names in pairs (melt/freeze, vaporise/condense, sublime/deposit).
On heating/cooling curves, flat = change of state; sloped = temperature of one phase changing.
Say 'average kinetic energy' when linking temperature to particles, not just 'particles move faster'.
In 'explain the heating curve' answers, name what is overcome: intermolecular forces for molecular substances, but ionic or metallic bonding for ionic solids and metals.

linkingQuestions.prompt: Why do substances with stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to change state?
